phonemes.desc: Open back vowel [u] with alveolar tap [ɾ]; the colonial spelling ‘Urca-’ reflects Quechua urqu, ‘mountain; within the earth’.
Voiceless velar stop [k] between open vowels — Quechua k, written c before a in the old orthography.
Labio-velar glide [wa]: colonial gu before a stands for the semivowel w (modern orthography would write wa).
Alveolar tap [ɾ] with close vowel [i]; the final element is related to Quechua quri, ‘gold’.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OOR-kah-wah-ree' — four light syllables; the 'g' is only the glide w and the final y a short 'ee'. Stress placement is not recorded: the initial stress follows modern Quechua habit and is a convention, not a fact.

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: urqu — ‘mountain; that which is beneath or within the earth’ — the first element of the name (Mannheim, The Language of the Inka since the European Invasion)

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: quri — ‘gold’ — the second element, the metal of his treasury (colonial dictionaries; Mannheim)

kin.label: Later tradition
kin.form: Hurkaway — the guardian serpent of Uku Pacha, the world within the earth, identified in later Andean tradition with Urcaguary

pronunciation.note: Urcaguary is Tier 2: the restored form carries no diacritic or distinctive letter beyond the capital, and the pre-conquest pronunciation is irrecoverable — even the stress is a modern convention. The catalog's gloss ‘He of the underground’ follows the reading of the name from Quechua urqu and quri; both are ordinary living words, which is why the figure's title and domain are one.

domains.title: Urcaguary
domains.subtitle: Underworld Jewels
domains.lead: Urcaguary is the Inca guardian of what lies beneath the mountains: gold, silver, emeralds and the other precious things sealed in the earth. The figure is known only through the colonial chronicle tradition and later folklore, and the sources are late, brief and partly modern — but they agree on the core: the underground hoard has a watcher, and it is not a vault, it is a god.

cards.name: Guardian of the Hoard
cards.desc: Beneath the mountains Urcaguary keeps the metals and gems of the inner earth; the traditional description hangs gold chains and precious stones from the serpent's tail.

cards.name: The Serpent with a Deer's Head
cards.desc: The figure takes the body of a serpent and the head of a taruka, the Andean deer — wealth that watches and thinks like a mountain animal.

cards.name: He of the Underground
cards.desc: The name reads from Quechua urqu, ‘within the earth’, and quri, ‘gold’: the title is the domain, and the domain is the treasury.

cards.name: The Treasure That Judges
cards.desc: The hoard belongs to the guardian, not the miner: in the moral economy of the Andean mine, gold is taken only as tribute, never as theft.

symbols.name: Gold chains
symbols.meaning: Hung from the serpent's tail in the chroniclers' descriptions — wealth worn as the guardian's own ornament

symbols.name: Emeralds and precious stones
symbols.meaning: The green gems of the Andes stored in the subterranean house the serpent keeps

symbols.name: The taruka (Andean deer) head
symbols.meaning: The alert head he wears: the deer of the high puna, watchful and unreachable

symbols.name: The serpent body
symbols.meaning: The winding form that coils through the veins of ore inside the mountains

symbols.name: The mountain vault
symbols.meaning: Every sealed vein and hidden pocket of ore is a door of his treasury

mythology.lead: Urcaguary has no surviving epic. The sources are late, brief and partly modern, and honesty requires saying so plainly. What the tradition preserves is a portrait rather than a cycle: a serpent-bodied watcher below the mountains, a theology of treasure, and a mining etiquette that is still practiced in the Andes.

myths.title: A God Seen Through Colonial Eyes
myths.text:
Everything securely known about Urcaguary descends from the chroniclers writing after the conquest — above all Martín de Murúa, whose Historia general del Piru (1616) catalogues the gods of the Andes, and Bernabé Cobo, whose Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653) preserves the most orderly account of the Inca huacas. In their pages Urcaguary appears as the deity of metals, jewels and the other precious things hidden underground — a figure who presided over ore-rich mountains and mining shrines, but whose cult left no standing temple and whose myths were never written down in Quechua. The colonial writers worked decades after the religion they described had been outlawed, from informants under missionary pressure, so their catalogues are triage documents as much as testimonies.

Read that way, Urcaguary is half-known by necessity: a god glimpsed through the gap between destroyed shrines and Spanish notebooks. The temple built here is therefore a temple over an archive, not over a ruin.

myths.title: The Serpent in the Veins of Gold
myths.text:
Later tradition gives the figure a body. Urcaguary is pictured as a great serpent with the head of a taruka, the Andean deer, gold chains and precious stones linked along the tail, dwelling beneath the mountains in the uku pacha, the world within the earth. The deer's head is explained as a mark of the guardian's way of thinking — alert, swift, impossible to catch — and in the same layer of folklore the guardian serpent of the depths, Hurkaway, is identified with Urcaguary: the snake that coils through the ore veins is the treasure's own watchman made visible.

The image is exact theology in zoological form. A vault guards wealth with walls; a serpent guards it with intention. The Andes buried their treasure in the most guarded shape the animal world offers.

myths.title: Offering Before the Blast
myths.text:
The etiquette the colonial writers describe at mining shrines still survives in the Andes, where ethnographers from the twentieth century to the present record miners pouring chicha, laying coca leaves and burning cigarettes for the powers of the mine before a single charge is set — the same ritual courtesy, the ch'alla, that crews in Potosí and the central Andes pay to the lord of the mountain and to the Tío, the old one of the deep workings. Urcaguary stands behind this courtesy as its theological ground: the underground metals belong first to the guardian, and gifts earn a share. Mining, in this ethics, is not extraction but tribute.

The rite turns an act of violence into a negotiation, and that is the whole lesson of the god: the earth parts for those who ask and swallows those who only take.

myths.title: The Gold That Cannot Be Stolen
myths.text:
The tradition's moral edge is aimed at thieves: Urcaguary protects the hoard from evil people who dare to steal it. After the conquest, when the ransom of Atahualpa filled a room with gold and the furnaces of Cuzco and Cajamarca melted down the sun god's garden and the huancas of the shrines, Andean storytellers had every reason to sharpen the point — the metal pried from the temples was only surface; the deep treasure has a serpent on watch, and it does not travel. Whether the tale circulated in exactly this form in the sixteenth century cannot now be shown, but the sentiment is old and Andean: gold is not owned, it is kept.

It is the theology of every robbed sanctuary, and it is also simply true: the empire's gold crossed the ocean; the guardian's never left the mountain.

lore.syncretism: Urcaguary's afterlife is a history of translations. Colonial missionaries folded the spirits of the uku pacha into Christian demonology — Supay, lord of the inner world, became the very word for devil in Quechua — while the miners kept the old courtesies under new names. The serpent body invited comparison with the amaru, the sacred Andean serpent of water, earth and the underworld, and in regional folklore the two guardians of the deep merge and separate: sometimes the amaru carries the treasure, sometimes Urcaguary carries the amaru's shape. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century compilations detached the figure from cult context entirely, presenting it as a ‘god of treasure’ in the European fairy-hoard sense, and modern summaries go further still, calling the gender ambiguous — a flattening the chronicles, which say little either way, cannot support. Read through all three layers, Urcaguary is best understood as the Inca theology of subterranean wealth caught mid-translation into European categories.
lore.culturalLegacy: The etiquette Urcaguary presides over is alive: Andean miners still offer coca, alcohol and smoke to the mountain and to the Tío of the workings before blasting, a rite documented ethnographically from Potosí across Bolivia and Peru for over a century. In folklore collections the name circulates as the guardian of hidden treasure — the tesoros ocultos whose gold turns to leaves in the hands of the unworthy, a pan-Andean motif his serpent keeps. In the museums of Cuzco and Lima the legacy is an absence: the gold and silver he hypothetically guarded, described at length by Cobo and Murúa, was melted into ingots within decades of the conquest, and his treasury survives only as chronicle. For Quechua language revival the name's elements remain living words — urqu, the mountain, and quri, gold — so the god's title is still pronounceable as a sentence of modern Quechua.
lore.extendedMeditation: What does it mean that a civilization gave its wealth a god? The Greeks gave Hermes to commerce and the Romans gave Juno Moneta to the mint; the Inca gave Urcaguary to gold that was still in the earth. That choice contains a complete economics. Gold's natural place, the figure says, is inside the mountain, where it is sacred; extraction is not sin but negotiation, and the negotiation never ends, because ownership never begins. The serpent with the deer's head is posted at a boundary the modern world refuses to see — the line between the surface we live on and the interior we dig into. Every blast re-asks his question in dynamite grammar: did you ask, or did you only take? A civilization that must give its minerals a guardian has admitted something the ledger never records.

sources.name: Martín de Murúa, Historia general del Piru (1616) — the colonial catalogue of Andean gods
Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653) — the fullest orderly account of the Inca huacas
Bruce Mannheim, The Language of the Inka since the European Invasion (1991) — the Quechua elements urqu and quri

lore.archaeology: No temple, cult statue or offering securely attributable to Urcaguary survives; the figure's archaeology is textual. The chronicles describe the golden effigies and huancas of the Coricancha and of provincial shrines — works seized and melted between 1533 and the 1570s, known today only through Cobo, Murúa and Cieza de León. Mining archaeology supplies the milieu: pre-Hispanic workings at Potosí's Cerro Rico and across the central Andes, stone hammers, ore-processing floors and shaft burials that kept the mountain's dead close to its metal. Andean art gives the iconography of his form without the name — serpents and deer crowd Moche and Inca metalwork and rock art — but no piece can be assigned to this deity with confidence.
